blocks.text: I was very excited to attempt making the box, and ultimately used it to store some candy a friend got from Carbone. The candy was pretty good.

blocks.alt: The finished wooden box with its lid slid aside to show wrapped candy.

blocks.text: The process of making the box was very simple. I worked on it with another student and we both guided each other through the process, along with some guidance from a member of the shop staff. Below are the steps we took.
1. Found a scrap piece of wood and cut it in half using bandsaw. We turned on the machine that sucks up dust but I still felt as though I inhaled a lot-- maybe time to stock up on masks.

blocks.alt: Sped-up, silent clip of cutting the wood with a bandsaw.

blocks.text: 2. I then drilled a hole on the box. In hingsight, this hole was too close to the edge given that I decided to sand the lid.

3. After drilling the hole, I cut the box horizontally in a ~4:1 ratio, again using the bandsaw. This created the lid. This process was a bit finnicky and I needed to be better with stabilization during this process. Alas.

4. After this, I sanded the bottom of the box (where stuff goes) to be straight. However, I was too aggressive with this process and ended up getting some slanted sides. For the top, I hastily sanded it to get rounded corners-- I did not feel compelled to be perfect and a quick glance would not see much defects.

blocks.alt: Sped-up, silent clip of sanding the wooden box.

blocks.text: 5. Then, using the drill press and forstner bits, I made the hole in the box to store stuff.

5. It took me a bit time to find the right screw to finish out the creation of the “lid.” Ultimately I still failed. The screw and the hole drilled for the screw were not made in tandem, which is a good (and perhaps obvious) learning for the future.
Ultimately, I am still happy with the box, given I have made something without instructions to refer to. I did not take any notes during Phil’s presentation and things ended up okay.

blocks.text: Similar to the box, I was very excited for this project. Unfortunately, I attempted something far too complex, achieved very disappointing results, and only produced one object of the five that I was to make.

images.alt: The finished wooden saucer seen from above, with uneven square recesses.
An angled view of the wooden saucer on a tiled table.

text: My theme for this semester is
, which is a uniquely American architectural style that emphasizes polychromatic coloring, exaggerated human forms, setback reliefs, and clocks. For this project, I specifically focused on

, which means there are lots of setbacks in the building. The Empire State Building and the American Radiator are classic examples of this style. That being said, I was not willing to make an entire building or even a model of one, so I decided to make a saucer, where instead of a curve, it was as though you were trying to make a curved base with only 4 angles.
This idea was entirely my own, but came after some
. Below are some drawings I made, which I gave as context to Codex:

blocks.alt: Whiteboard sketches of the pine slab, square saucer and stepped cross-section.

blocks.text: Along with ideation, Codex was especially useful for generating a Blender file that allowed me to visualize what I had in mind and made it easy to play around with my assumptions. The Blender file looked like this:

images.alt: Isometric render of the pine saucer with four nested square steps.
Angled view of the saucer model in Blender.
Top view of the square saucer model in Blender.
Editable Blender dimensions for the outer square, thickness, drop and ledges, in inches.

blocks.text: In mind, the process for this was fairly simple: I would measure out each recessed section, each increasing in length and depth as they got closer to the base (see above for exact dimensions), draw lines, and then use the drill press to make the various sections.

In practice, I not only struggled immensely with drawing straight lines, the drilling process took over 100 holes and an amount of precision I did not possess. Additionally, while you were very helpful in terms of figuring out how to make precise the drilling process, I found it very difficult to actually eyeball the exact place the drill was at all times. As a result, the saucer has clear levels, but which are incredibly uneven.

blocks.alt: Silent looping clip of drilling the wooden saucer.

blocks.text: The below is a GIF of the various jigs I made simply to draw the lines, which ended up being dramatically uneven despite this Rube Goldberg-esque process.

blocks.alt: Eight photos of rulers, clamps and wooden jigs used to mark the saucer, shown in the original order.

blocks.text: After drilling the recesses in, the “saucer” I made was incredibly uneven and filled with holes. This was planned for, and I tried my hand at two types of Dremels, one sandpaper and one metal, to even things out. This was the most satisfying part of this process, and it gave my woodwork some resemblance to what was created in Blender. Still, the result is quite rough.

I am sorry that I did not get to create all 5. At 9:45PM today I had the idea of using clippers and saws to make the recessed levels, which would have possibly produced a more precise and aesthetically pleasing result. Unfortunately, I lacked the willpower to stay up to finish out all 5.

This process has been a humbling lesson in the limits of converting imagination to reality. Still, I know this project would have been possible with access and knowledge of how to use a CNC machine, which I will perhaps do to redeem myself in the future.
I remain incredibly excited for future projects in this class.
